name: Phenol / Baker-Gordon peel
lead: The phenol or Baker-Gordon peel is a deep chemical peel in which a mixture containing phenol and croton oil is applied to the skin to produce a controlled deep injury, after which new skin regenerates. People seek it to smooth coarse wrinkling, reduce sun damage and soften some scarring, aiming for tighter, smoother, more even-looking facial skin than lighter peels produce.[1][2]

Chemical peeling goes back to the second half of the nineteenth century, when Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra used phenol, croton oil and nitric acid for freckles and skin irregularities. Wikipedia states that phenol-croton oil peels were used discreetly by early Hollywood stars in the 1920s and entered mainstream practice in the 1960s through Thomas Baker and Howard Gordon; Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, gives 1961 for the Baker-Gordon formula.[1][2] Today the term "phenol-croton oil peel" has replaced the vaguer "phenol peel" in the medical literature, and croton oil is considered the active ingredient behind the intense exfoliating reaction.[1]

Both sources describe the peel as carrying more risk than lighter peels, including cardiac and pigmentation effects, and it is performed by medical providers under sedation or anaesthesia.[1][2] A 2024 dermatology review of chemical peels lists deep and segmental phenol approaches among the categories it covers.[3]

chain: Phenol and croton oil injure the skin deeply and in a controlled way
Skin regenerates over days to weeks
Fewer deep wrinkles and a smoother, more even surface
angle.text: The peel is used by people who want a stronger skin-resurfacing result than light or medium peels provide, targeting deep lines, sun damage and some scars on the face.

infobox: 1960s into mainstream practice (Baker and Gordon); 1961 per Grokipedia[1][2]

paras: Wikipedia credits von Hebra (1816-1880) with introducing chemical peeling in the later nineteenth century using phenol, croton oil and nitric acid, and says the phenol-croton oil peel was used clandestinely by Hollywood stars in the 1920s before Thomas Baker and Howard Gordon brought it into mainstream practice in the 1960s.[1]

Grokipedia attributes the introduction of phenol as a peeling agent to William Tilbury Fox in 1871 and a description of its peeling properties to Paul Unna in 1882, and dates the Baker-Gordon formula to 1961 (88% phenol with croton oil, hexachlorophene soap and water). It is AI-generated and may contain errors, and Wikipedia is preferred where they differ.[2]

Wikipedia classifies phenol-croton oil as the deep peel, the most intense among peels that range from alpha-hydroxy acids through salicylic and retinoic acid peels to trichloroacetic acid. It notes that early phenol peels were very painful and often performed under general anaesthesia, while newer formulations allow variable depth and sedation with local anaesthetic.[1] Grokipedia describes the Baker-Gordon formula as a benchmark for profound resurfacing because of its consistent depth.[2]
Wikipedia states that complications rise with peel depth and lists photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment change, milia, skin atrophy, texture change and scarring among them.[1]

Dermatology reviews describe skin depigmentation from chemical agents, and report that contact with phenol or resorcinol may cause exogenous ochronosis, a blue-black pigmentation, in dark-skinned individuals.[4][5]

Grokipedia reports that systemic phenol absorption can cause arrhythmias and cardiotoxicity, especially with pre-existing heart disease or large treated areas, and that laryngeal spasm and renal and pulmonary toxicity have been described. It describes frequent and possibly permanent hypopigmentation, particularly in lighter skin, higher scarring potential leading to the peel generally being limited to once per area, and infection and herpes reactivation. It lists pre-procedure ECG and organ function tests, cardiac monitoring, intravenous fluids and application in timed segments as described precautions.[2] These details come from an AI-generated page whose citations are not all clearly matched to its claims.

The peel is categorised on the wiki under hardmaxx as an invasive resurfacing procedure with a reputation for significant downsides. Forum posts discussing skin-lightening peels note that phenol peels are generally considered unsuitable for darker skin, in line with the pigment-change risks described above.[1][4]

timeline.event: William Tilbury Fox is credited with introducing phenol as a peeling agent (per Grokipedia).[2]
Phenol-croton oil peels reportedly used discreetly by early Hollywood stars.[1]
Baker and Gordon introduce their phenol-croton oil formula (per Grokipedia).[2]
Phenol-croton oil peeling enters mainstream practice through Baker and Gordon.[1]

card.summary: The deepest classic chemical peel, a phenol and croton oil mixture with documented cardiac and pigment risks, performed under medical supervision.
card.aka: Phenol-croton oil peel; deep chemical peel
card.note: Systemic absorption of phenol is reported to affect the heart; permanent lightening of skin is a reported effect.

quick.overview:
The Baker-Gordon peel is a deep chemical peel based on phenol and croton oil, introduced in the early 1960s. It is used to treat deep wrinkles, sun damage and some scarring, and is regarded in the medical literature as the strongest of the traditional peels.

Because of its depth, descriptions emphasise medical supervision, sedation or anaesthesia and monitoring, and a long recovery. In looksmaxxing discussions it is a rare, high-stakes procedure.
quick.mechanism: Phenol acts as a caustic, keratolytic agent that destroys the outer skin layers, and croton oil is described as the active ingredient that increases penetration. The injury is followed by skin regeneration over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Reported risks include heart rhythm disturbances from systemic phenol absorption, permanent hypopigmentation, scarring, infection and herpes reactivation. Wikipedia notes that the deeper the peel, the more complications can arise. Descriptions of the procedure recommend cardiac monitoring and note it is generally limited to a single treatment per area.
